modules.title: Loss is a fitness function: gradient descent vs evolution
objectives: Explain training as minimising a loss over billions of weights, in plain words
Compare gradient descent (follow the local slope) with an evolutionary strategy (mutate, select, repeat)
Predict how step size / mutation size and landscape ruggedness change the outcome
modules.analogy: Fitness landscape, hill-climbing populations, local optima, Wright’s shifting balance
modules.lab: In-browser fitness-landscape widget (GD vs ES), then ask Claude Code/Codex to write and run a short Python script that repeats the comparison across 50 random starts and reports success rates.

questions.q: In next-word training, what plays the role of the fitness function, and what plays the role of the genotype?
questions.a: The loss (how wrong the model's next-word predictions are on real text) is the fitness function, inverted: lower is better. The genotype is the set of weights. Training changes one set of weights step by step; it doesn't select among a population.

questions.q: Why does gradient descent need far fewer evaluations than the evolution strategy in the widget, and why does that matter at the scale of billions of weights?
questions.a: Each gradient step uses the exact local direction of improvement, while the ES has to discover a direction by sampling λ mutants and keeping the best. With billions of weights, random mutations almost never point downhill, but backpropagation gives the full gradient cheaply.

questions.q: You raised ruggedness and gradient descent started stalling. Name one change that helps the evolutionary strategy and one risk of simply raising gradient descent's step size.
questions.a: A larger mutation size σ (or more offspring λ) lets the ES jump over small ridges into better basins. A bigger learning rate can carry gradient descent over ridges too, but it can also make it overshoot, bounce around, or skip past the global basin.

questions.q: A post quotes a precise “generalization gap” for a frontier model with no source. How should you use it?
questions.a: Keep the concept (flat basins tend to generalise better than sharp minima) and treat the specific numbers as unverified until you find a primary source. Promotional threads are pointers, not evidence.

modules.built: A working mental model of training as loss minimisation, plus a reusable script that races gradient descent against an evolution strategy across landscape ruggedness.

modules.title: Mutation rate: tokens, next-token distributions and temperature
objectives: Describe generation as repeated sampling from a next-token probability distribution
Explain what temperature (and top-p) do to that distribution and why outputs vary between runs
Choose temperature settings for creative vs extraction/classification work
modules.analogy: Mutation rate and drift: low rates conserve, high rates explore and accumulate noise
modules.lab: Temperature-sampler widget, then a Claude Code/Codex lab: run the same prompt 10 times at two settings via a local script or the CLI, and measure answer diversity.

questions.q: What does the model actually output at each generation step, before any word is chosen?
questions.a: A score for every token in its vocabulary, which is turned into a probability distribution over the next token. A sampler then picks one token, appends it, and the process repeats.

questions.q: What does temperature 0 do, and why might two runs of an agent still differ?
questions.a: Temperature 0 means greedy decoding: always take the most probable token. Runs can still differ because hosted inference isn't guaranteed to be exactly repeatable, and in agents any small difference early on compounds over many steps (plus tools and environments change).

questions.q: Kev stores a fitted “temperature” in each checkpoint. Why doesn't it change which answer wins, and what is it for?
questions.a: Dividing every score by the same positive number keeps their order, so the top answer stays the same. The calibration temperature only rescales confidence, so that “90% sure” really means right about 90% of the time on held-out data.

questions.q: You're extracting species counts from scanned field sheets. Which sampling setting do you want, and what else do you need?
questions.a: Temperature 0 (deterministic, no exploration) plus a schema and an instruction never to guess numbers, as in the local-LLM course's extraction example. And you still need verification, because low temperature makes the model consistent, not correct.

questions.q: Give one way the “temperature = mutation rate” analogy breaks.
questions.a: Mutations are heritable and selection acts on them over generations. Temperature only reshapes one draw at one step: nothing is inherited, and nothing is selected unless you add a selection step such as best-of-n with a verifier.

modules.built: A sampling intuition you can tune with a slider, and a script that measures how much a model's answers vary with prompt specificity.

modules.title: Reading the organism: confidence, calibration and controlled language
objectives: Distinguish a model’s stated confidence from calibrated probability
Use output formats that make errors easier to spot (controlled language, diagrams, HTML explainers)
Run a small calibration check on a yes/no task
modules.analogy: Phenotype vs genotype: you only observe behaviour, so you design assays that reveal the underlying state
modules.lab: Ask your coding agent to build a 40-item yes/no question set from your field, collect answers with stated confidence, and plot a reliability diagram.

questions.q: A model is right on 80% of questions. Is it calibrated?
questions.a: You can't tell from accuracy alone. It's calibrated only if its stated confidence matches its hit rate. For example, the answers it gives at 0.9 should be right about 90% of the time and the ones at 0.6 about 60%. An 80%-accurate model that says 0.99 on everything is overconfident.

questions.q: Kev fits a temperature on held-out data. What can that fix, and what can't it fix?
questions.a: It rescales confidence so that probabilities match observed accuracy, which lowers calibration error and the number of confident wrong answers. It can't change which answer wins or reorder which answers the model is more or less sure of, so a model that ranks its right and wrong answers badly stays bad at that.

questions.q: Why include unanswerable questions in a calibration test?
questions.a: They catch the most dangerous behaviour: confidently answering when the evidence isn't there. A well-calibrated system should give low confidence (or abstain) on them. Kev's benchmark reports how often a model still answers them at 0.9 or higher.

questions.q: You want an agent to auto-accept species IDs it is sure about and send the rest to you. What must you do before choosing the threshold?
questions.a: Measure it on your own labelled data: check accuracy at each confidence level (a reliability diagram) and pick the threshold that keeps the error rate among auto-accepted cases within your budget. Don't trust a vendor's number or a self-reported “confidence” field without testing.

questions.q: How does Karpathy's ASD-STE100 tip relate to calibration?
questions.a: Calibration tells you how often to distrust an answer. Controlled language (and diagrams or HTML) makes the answer easier to check claim by claim, so you find the errors faster when you do distrust it.

modules.built: A calibration assay (reliability diagram, Brier score, ECE, unknowable-question check) for a model's stated confidence, plus your Unit 1 notebook indexing all three experiments.

modules.title: Carrying capacity: context windows, caching and compaction
objectives: Explain why every turn re-reads the whole conversation and what that costs
Describe compaction and why long sessions drift
Apply habits that keep context lean (one task per session, clear, plan first)
modules.analogy: Carrying capacity K: a habitat supports only so much before crowding degrades everyone
modules.lab: Measure it: ask Claude Code to report token use (/usage or /context) before and after a long exploratory session versus a fresh, scoped one; write down the difference.

questions.q: Why does an agent's token bill grow faster than the length of its conversation?
questions.a: Each call re-sends and re-reads the whole history, so the total tokens processed is the sum of all the context sizes along the way, which grows roughly quadratically with the number of turns. Caching makes repeated prefixes cheaper but doesn't change that shape.

questions.q: Name two things that break the prompt cache, and the fix for each.
questions.a: Changing the start of the prompt every step, such as a timestamp in the system prompt: put changing information at the end instead. Switching models mid-session: pick one model per session. (A long break also lets the cache expire: summarise, then start fresh.)

questions.q: In the OpenHands data, what took up the largest share of agent context?
questions.a: Tool results (37%), such as file contents and command output, followed by the system prompt and tool descriptions (23%). The model's replies to the user were only 2%.

questions.q: Why can a compaction method pass a benchmark and still fail in real use?
questions.a: The benchmark may not contain the situations compaction destroys. OpenHands's benchmark had single-turn tasks, so it never tested forgetting mid-conversation instructions or remembering that a pull request had already been opened. Real use did both.

questions.q: A rule like “never touch the production database” must survive a six-hour session. Where should it live?
questions.a: In a pinned file that the agent re-reads after every reset (and in the system prompt), not only in the chat history, where compaction can summarise it away.

modules.built: A before/after measurement of your own agent's context use (crowded vs compacted vs scoped), and a set of habits that keep the window lean.

modules.title: A map, not a manual: CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and progressive disclosure
objectives: Write a short instructions file that points to deeper docs instead of containing them
Use nested instruction files and on-demand loading (progressive disclosure)
Recognise the failure modes of one giant instructions file
modules.analogy: A field guide’s dichotomous key: a few questions route you to the right detailed page
modules.lab: Have your coding agent interview you and draft a ≤100-line CLAUDE.md + docs/ folder for your capstone repo; then test it by asking three questions in a fresh session.

questions.q: Give three reasons a single huge AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md tends to fail.
questions.a: It crowds the scarce context window, so the task and code get less room. When everything is marked important nothing is, so it stops guiding. It goes stale fast and can't easily be checked mechanically, so wrong rules linger and get followed.

questions.q: What is progressive disclosure, in one sentence?
questions.a: Give the agent a small, stable entry point (a map) that tells it where to look next, so it loads detailed docs only when the task needs them instead of loading everything up front.

questions.q: You keep correcting the agent about the same date format. What should you do?
questions.a: Put the rule in the instruction file or the relevant doc (if you've corrected it twice, it belongs there). Better still, add a check that fails when the format is wrong, so the rule is enforced rather than merely suggested.

questions.q: Why does the OpenAI team say knowledge in chat threads or people's heads “doesn't exist” for the agent?
questions.a: The agent can only use what's in its context or what it can reach in the repository. Decisions made elsewhere are invisible to it until they're written into versioned files it can read.

questions.q: How can one map serve both Claude Code and Codex?
questions.a: Write the map in AGENTS.md, which Codex reads, and make CLAUDE.md import it with an @AGENTS.md line, so Claude Code loads the same content.

modules.built: Your capstone repository with a ≤100-line AGENTS.md map, four focused docs, and a check script that fails when the map points at something that no longer exists.

modules.title: Prompts that work: specificity, questions first, plan then build
objectives: Turn a vague request into a specific, checkable prompt
Use “ask me questions first” and plan-then-execute patterns
Use codebase Q&A as a safe first use of an agent
modules.analogy: Experimental design: a well-specified protocol beats a vague hypothesis
modules.lab: Rewrite three of your recent real prompts using the patterns, run old vs new in Claude Code or Codex, and score the outputs against a 3-point rubric.

questions.q: What three parts does the Claude Code guide say a good prompt needs?
questions.a: A goal, a scope and a done criterion. For example: reproduce the bug with a test (goal), fix it in the validation layer only (scope), and don't stop until all tests pass (done).

questions.q: Why does Boris recommend codebase Q&A as the first use of a coding agent?
questions.a: It's safe, because nothing is edited, and it teaches you how to prompt and where the agent's abilities end before you trust it with changes. It's also directly useful: at Anthropic it shortened technical onboarding from weeks to days.

questions.q: Why is “ask me questions before you start” cheaper than writing a very long prompt?
questions.a: A long prompt is re-read on every turn of the session, while a short intent plus a few multiple-choice answers carries the same information in fewer tokens. It also surfaces the gaps you didn't know you'd left.

questions.q: The agent says “Done, everything works.” What should your prompt have included to make that claim checkable?
questions.a: A done criterion that a command can verify, such as a test suite that passes or output that matches a reference file, plus a request to run it and show the result. Without that, “done” is just the agent's opinion.

questions.q: How does the field-protocol analogy break?
questions.a: A field team or reviewer usually questions a vague protocol before data collection starts. An agent fills gaps with confident guesses and starts immediately, so you have to build the questioning and planning steps into the prompt or the instruction file yourself.

modules.built: Three before/after prompt rewrites with rubric scores, and version 2 of your capstone map with a “How to work here” protocol (the Unit 2 build).

modules.title: Organism = genome + body: model and harness anatomy
objectives: Name the seven harness subsystems (loop, LLM layer, tools, memory, safety, orchestration, extensions)
Explain the core loop: call model, run tool or finish, check the exit condition
Diagnose a failure by locating the missing layer
modules.analogy: Genome (model weights) plus body plan (harness): appendages are tools, metabolism is the loop
modules.lab: Ask Claude Code or Codex to explain its own harness: which tools it has, how it decides to stop, where memory lives. Map its answers onto the seven-part blueprint.

questions.q: What does “agent = model + harness” mean in practice?
questions.a: The model only turns tokens into tokens. Everything else that makes it act (the loop, tool execution, prompt assembly, memory, permissions, sub-agents, extensions) is the harness. If a component isn't the model, it's part of the harness.

questions.q: Describe the core agent loop and two common exit conditions.
questions.a: Send the model the task plus history; if it requests a tool, run the tool, append the result and call the model again; repeat. Exit when the model replies without a tool call or calls a final-output tool, or when a turn cap, budget or error stops it.

questions.q: Name the seven harness subsystems from the source-code study.
questions.a: Agent loop, LLM integration, tools and actions, memory and context, safety and permissions, orchestration (sub-agents), and extensibility (hooks, skills, plugins, MCP).

questions.q: The study found a 100-line harness reporting benchmark results in the same range as million-line ones. What does the extra size buy?
questions.a: Production readiness rather than raw task success: safety and sandboxing, recovery from failures, cost control, extensibility and user experience.

questions.q: An agent's patches keep reaching your review with failing tests. Which layer do you fix first, and how?
questions.a: Verification: add a check that runs the tests and rejects the patch before it reaches you, and define done as “tests pass” rather than “the agent says it's done”.

modules.built: A seven-part dissection of your own coding agent, saved as `docs/harness.md` in your capstone. It's the blueprint for the harness you'll build tomorrow.

modules.title: Build a minimal organism: a 100-line agent loop
objectives: Implement a loop with two tools, a turn cap and a state file
See how tool results are fed back as tokens
Understand why minimal harnesses are dangerous without guardrails
modules.analogy: A minimal cell: the smallest set of parts that can sense, act and persist
modules.lab: With your coding agent, build agent.py (two tools: read_file, list_dir; max 8 turns; STATE.md), run it on a small folder, then add a third tool.

questions.q: How does a model “call” a tool in your agent.py?
questions.a: It writes a JSON object naming the tool and its arguments as plain text. The harness parses it, runs the real function, and appends the result to the history as text, which the model reads on the next turn.

questions.q: Why does the prompt grow every turn, and what does that cost?
questions.a: Each turn the harness re-sends the rules, the task and the whole history, including every tool result so far. So the tokens read per turn rise steadily and the total rises roughly quadratically, which is why tool results are truncated and turns are capped.

questions.q: What does Ouro demonstrate, and what does its author warn about?
questions.a: That a capable model with one prompt and one powerful tool (eval) can bootstrap its own agent loop and extend itself. He warns it has no guardrails or permissions, may never return or may not bootstrap at all, and should only be run in an isolated container.

questions.q: Why is the path check inside the tool rather than just an instruction in the prompt?
questions.a: Instructions can be ignored, misread or summarised away; code that refuses paths outside the root always runs. Safety boundaries belong in the harness, enforced deterministically, not in the model's good intentions.

questions.q: The harness paper recommends starting with only a bash tool. Why did today's lab avoid bash?
questions.a: Bash can do anything (delete, send, install), and a minimal loop has no permission system to limit it. Read-only, root-checked tools give a safe first organism. Add action tools only with permissions or sandboxing in place.

modules.built: `harness/agent.py`: a working ~100-line agent loop with three read-only tools, a root boundary, a turn cap and a STATE.md log. It's the core of your capstone's harness.

modules.title: Behavioural repertoires: workflows versus autonomous agents
objectives: Tell a fixed workflow from an agent that chooses its own steps
Use the classic patterns: prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer
Pick the simplest pattern that solves a task
modules.analogy: Fixed action patterns versus flexible foraging behaviour
modules.lab: Solve one literature-triage task twice (a prompt chain and a free agent) with your coding agent; compare cost, time and error rate on 20 abstracts.

questions.q: What distinguishes a workflow from an agent in Anthropic's definition?
questions.a: In a workflow, models and tools run through predefined code paths that you wrote. In an agent, the model dynamically decides its own steps and tool use.

questions.q: Name the five workflow patterns and one situation suited to each.
questions.a: Prompt chaining (fixed steps, such as outline then check then write); routing (distinct categories, such as easy vs hard queries); parallelisation (independent sections, or voting for confidence); orchestrator-workers (unpredictable subtasks, such as multi-file code changes); evaluator-optimizer (clear criteria where critique helps, such as polishing a translation).

questions.q: Why might a fixed pipeline beat an autonomous agent on a well-defined task?
questions.a: It's cheaper and faster (no tokens spent deciding what to do next), more consistent run to run, and each step can be inspected and checked. Evidence like the Agentless pipeline shows fixed pipelines can be competitive even on coding benchmarks.

questions.q: When do you actually need an agent?
questions.a: When the task is open-ended, you can't predict the number or kind of steps, and you can't hard-code the path, and when you can sandbox it, cap it and verify its output.

questions.q: How does the fixed-action-pattern analogy break?
questions.a: Selection fixed animal routines over generations and running them costs nothing extra. You choose the pattern per task, and flexibility is paid for in tokens and unpredictability on every run. Unlike an animal, you can also inspect and test a workflow's steps.

modules.built: A labelled 20-abstract triage set in your capstone and a script that compares a gated prompt chain with a free agent on accuracy, calls and time.

modules.title: Reflex and cortex: model routers and cheap decision layers
objectives: Explain why routine yes/no decisions should not go to the most expensive model
Design a router with tiers, criteria and a classifier
Measure a router with offline evals and an A/B comparison
modules.analogy: Spinal reflex arcs versus cortical deliberation: fast cheap circuits handle routine stimuli
modules.lab: Add a router to your agent: a cheap model (or rules) classifies each task into a tier; log choices to CSV and score 20 tasks.

questions.q: In LangChain's A/B test, what happened to quality and cost when they routed instead of always using the strongest model?
questions.a: Quality showed no measurable change (29.2% vs 27.3% of threads ended in a merged PR, p = 0.49), while median cost per thread fell 64% ($0.94 vs $2.61). Most threads went to the balanced and fast tiers.

questions.q: Why did their router pick a model once per thread instead of on every turn?
questions.a: Switching models mid-thread discards the prompt cache, so the new model re-reads the whole history at full price. That can wipe out the savings, and routing per turn also adds a classifier call on every turn.

questions.q: What are the three parts of their router?
questions.a: A base prompt (pick the least expensive model likely to complete the task), plain-language criteria for each tier, and a classifier model that reads the request and picks a tier.

questions.q: Why are under-routes worse than over-routes, and why are they hard to notice?
questions.a: An under-route gives a hard task to a model that can't do it well, which costs rework or ships a worse result. Over-routes only waste money. Under-routes fail silently, as plausible but worse answers, so you only see them if you track outcomes.

questions.q: Two decision-layer projects removed or stopped recommending their routers. What's the general lesson?
questions.a: A router is a hypothesis that must be evaluated against the right baseline, such as one strong agent or the main model's own choice. Gains on a weak baseline, or on scripted examples, may vanish in real sessions.

modules.built: A labelled routing eval set, a rules router and a model router scored for agreement and under-routing, and `--tier auto` in your agent: the Unit 3 harness, complete with tools, turn cap and router.

modules.title: Feedback loops: loop engineering and stopping rules
objectives: Write a loop contract: job, trigger, state, verifier, stop rule, approval
Loop on evidence (tests, checks), not on the model’s confidence
Set budgets: attempts, time, tokens
modules.analogy: Homeostatic feedback loops and density-dependent regulation
modules.lab: Have your coding agent write a headless loop (claude -p or codex exec) that re-runs a failing analysis script until its tests pass, with a 3-attempt cap and STATE.md.

questions.q: What makes something a loop rather than a scheduler, according to the Loops and Graphs course?
questions.a: A check that can fail the work without you present. Produce, check, correct, repeat until green. Without a check that can fail, you just have something running repeatedly.

questions.q: Why is “no errors were raised” not a valid check?
questions.a: The absence of an error isn't evidence of correctness: wrong output often runs without errors. A loop built on it can repeat a mistake until the budget runs out while every log line looks clean.

questions.q: List the six lines of the loop contract and the failure each prevents.
questions.a: Job (scope creep and vague work); trigger (when it runs); state (repeating yesterday's work); verifier (bad work getting through without you); stop (endless retries and spend); approval (irreversible actions without a human).

questions.q: Why cap attempts at about three instead of letting the loop keep trying?
questions.a: Repeated failure usually means the plan or the task specification is wrong, which the loop can't see. More attempts mostly burn tokens, so stop and escalate to a person with the evidence.

questions.q: Your loop always goes green on the first attempt. What should you suspect, and how do you test it?
questions.a: The verifier might be blind (always passing) or the agent might be editing the tests. Break it on purpose: feed it known-bad work or an impossible test and confirm it fails, and guard the test files (for example with a hash check).

modules.built: A six-line loop contract and `loops/fix_until_green.py`: a headless fix-until-green loop with a tamper check, a three-attempt cap, a STATE.md log and an escalation path, tested against a verifier that can't pass.

modules.title: Food chains to food webs: graph engineering
objectives: Break work into nodes with typed outputs and deterministic edges
Use fan-out/fan-in, gates, correction edges and learning edges
Keep the generator from grading its own work
modules.analogy: Trophic levels and energy flow between compartments
modules.lab: Build a small graph in plain Python (or LangGraph): split 30 records, annotate in parallel, merge with a code node, gate with an independent check.

questions.q: How do you tell a real edge from a fake one?
questions.a: Ask whether the next step actually reads the previous step's output: can you name the variable that crosses the arrow? If not, the two steps are independent and can run in parallel. The wait came only from the order you wrote them in.

questions.q: Name the four kinds of node and say which one should never be a model call.
questions.a: Splitter, worker, code node and gate. The code node (merge, rank, deduplicate, compare) should be plain code, because those operations have one correct answer and a model only adds cost, latency and variance.

questions.q: Why must a verifier have a fresh context, and why isn't that enough on its own?
questions.a: A verifier that sees the worker's reasoning tends to accept it, and models also tend to prefer their own outputs. A fresh context breaks that priming. But verifiers that all rely on the same source can agree without verifying anything, so you still need anchors: tests that ran, deterministic checks, frozen rules.

questions.q: What's the difference between a correction edge and a learning edge?
questions.a: A correction edge sends one failed unit back to its producer, with evidence and a narrow scope, to fix the current run. A learning edge turns an accepted result into a constraint in the splitter's brief, so every future run improves.

questions.q: 80% of your workflow is independent work and you run 8 workers. What speed-up should you expect at best?
questions.a: Amdahl's law: 1 / (0.2 + 0.8/8) = 1 / 0.3 ≈ 3.3×, not 8×. The serial parts (split, merge, gate) cap the gain.

modules.built: A field-data QA graph in plain Python: code splitter, parallel model workers with typed outputs, a code merge with a one-batch correction edge, a gate of deterministic rules plus a fresh-context verifier, a scored report, and a learning edge into `rules/brief.md`.

modules.title: Approve only the last step: hooks, headless runs and permissions
objectives: Use CLAUDE.md, permissions and plan mode to bound an agent
Add a hook that runs checks automatically after edits
Run agents headlessly for scheduled jobs
modules.analogy: Field-station protocols: routine sampling runs unattended, the PI signs off the final dataset
modules.lab: Set up a repo with a test hook and permissions, then run one task headlessly and review only the final diff.

questions.q: Why does the Claude Code guide say a hook is stronger than a line in CLAUDE.md?
questions.a: CLAUDE.md is loaded as instructions, which the model can forget or skip under load. A hook is executed by the harness at a fixed moment every time, regardless of what the model decides. That's the dual-encoding rule: words for intent, a mechanical gate for enforcement.

questions.q: Your headless job's agent prints “All done, everything works!” What should decide whether the change can be merged?
questions.a: The gate status: deterministic evidence such as the test exit code and a diff that stays inside the planned files, read by the harness. The agent's message is not evidence; a completion message should never unlock a merge.

questions.q: Why gate on blast radius rather than on the model's confidence score?
questions.a: Confidence is the only input the model itself can influence, so it's the weakest. Blast radius (how hard the mistake is to undo) is a property of the action. Contained, reversible work can flow automatically; hard-to-reverse actions get a lane that never opens, which unlike a threshold can't drift.

questions.q: You deny `rm` but the agent deletes a file using a Python one-liner. What went wrong, and what's the better fix?
questions.a: The rule was written against one command, not against the outcome. Agents follow literal permissions, so gaps get exploited by accident. Better fixes act at a level the agent can't route around: protect the folder (deny writes to `data/raw/`, or make it read-only), use a sandbox, and keep backups under version control.

questions.q: Where should the one human approval sit in an unattended workflow, and why not in the middle?
questions.a: At the step of highest consequence and lowest reversibility, such as the commit, merge or data release. A human approving intermediate steps becomes the slowest node, and the whole graph runs only as fast as a person reading.

modules.built: A field-QA repo with tests, permission rules and a test-running hook, plus one headless run whose only human step was your final commit: the Unit 4 build your capstone will reuse.

modules.title: Orchestration topologies: manager versus decentralised handoffs
objectives: Contrast the manager pattern (agents as tools) with decentralised handoffs
Use task decomposition and replanning
Decide when not to go multi-agent
modules.analogy: Eusocial colonies with a queen vs decentralised swarms (stigmergy)
modules.lab: Have your coding agent build an orchestrator that fans out three summariser subagents over papers, then synthesises; compare with a single agent.

questions.q: In the manager pattern and the decentralised pattern, what does an edge between two agents represent?
questions.a: In the manager pattern an edge is a tool call: the manager calls a worker and gets a result back, keeping control. In the decentralised pattern an edge is a handoff: control and the conversation state transfer one way to the peer, which takes over.

questions.q: OpenAI suggests splitting into several agents when there's “tool overload”. What actually causes the overload, and what should you try first?
questions.a: Overlap and similarity between tools more than their raw number. First try clearer tool names, parameters and descriptions; split into separate agents only if that doesn't fix the wrong tool choices.

questions.q: Give one gain and one loss of decomposing a task across agents, from the CMU lecture.
questions.a: Gain: each subtask needs less context, and cheaper or specialised models can handle some subtasks. Loss: the decomposition can miss details and is inflexible, and it's hard to pass exactly the right information between modules, whereas a single well-managed agent keeps all past actions available.

questions.q: In your orchestrator, why did the fan-in step use code rather than a model call?
questions.a: Parsing, validating keys, rejecting malformed replies and building a table have exactly one correct answer, so code does them with no cost, latency or variance. The model is saved for the cross-paper judgement in the synthesis step.

questions.q: How does the ant-colony picture mislead you about multi-agent systems?
questions.a: Colony coordination is evolved, robust and self-cleaning (trails evaporate). Agent topologies are designed and fragile: each added agent multiplies token cost and failure points, and shared state keeps stale or wrong entries unless you expire them.

modules.built: A manager-pattern orchestrator that fans three papers out to parallel summarisers, validates their output in code, and is measured against a single-agent baseline.

modules.title: Division of labour: subagents, teams and the adversary
objectives: Give subagents isolated context and restricted tools
Use an advisor or adversarial reviewer before “done”
Weigh team benefits against token cost and echo-chamber risk
modules.analogy: Castes and division of labour; predators that keep prey populations honest
modules.lab: Create a read-only reviewer subagent in Claude Code and run it on a data-cleaning change; log what it catches.

questions.q: Give two good reasons to use a subagent instead of the main conversation, and one reason not to.
questions.a: Good reasons: the task produces verbose output you don't want in your main context, you want to enforce tool restrictions, or the work is self-contained and can return a summary. Not: quick targeted changes or iterative back-and-forth work where phases share a lot of context (and a fresh subagent needs time to gather context).

questions.q: What are the three moments when an adversary or advisor is most useful?
questions.a: Before committing to a plan or locking an interface, when the same error comes back (are we fixing the cause or hiding the symptom?), and before declaring the task done.

questions.q: Four reviewers share one context window and all report the same issue. Why is that a problem, and what's the fix?
questions.a: They converged: the first finding anchored the rest, so you paid for four reviews and got one opinion with three echoes. Give each reviewer its own context and a distinct lens (or split the work along a dimension where each sees something different).

questions.q: When do Claude Code's docs say an agent team is better than subagents, and what does it cost?
questions.a: When workers need to share findings, challenge each other and coordinate on their own: research and review, competing-hypothesis debugging, separate modules. It costs significantly more tokens (each teammate has its own context, so cost scales with team size) plus coordination overhead.

questions.q: Why isn't a team of cloned agents like a caste system?
questions.a: Castes differ genuinely, so their errors are partly independent. Cloned agents share weights, training and often context, so they share blind spots. Diversity must be designed in through separate contexts, different lenses, deterministic checks or different models.

modules.built: A read-only reviewer subagent with a three-lens checklist, tested against a seeded “zeros are data” bug, plus the first rows of a review log your eval suite will reuse.

modules.title: A guild at work: role-based teams and prompt injection
objectives: Assign roles (planner, navigator, checker, guard, logger) for a real task
Defend against prompt injection from web content
Make multi-agent runs repeatable and logged
modules.analogy: Foraging guilds and mixed-species flocks with sentinels
modules.lab: Run a role-based browser or lookup team over a CSV of taxon names (e.g. checking a public database), with a guard role and a log.csv.

questions.q: Name the six roles in Hexo's browser team and the one habit that prevents 40 broken records.
questions.a: Planner, navigator, filler, checker, guard and logger. The habit: process three rows, stop, and inspect the log before continuing, because most broken runs fail on the first row or two.

questions.q: What is prompt injection, and why can't a sentence in CLAUDE.md alone stop it?
questions.a: Text inside data (a web page, a document, a CSV field) that the model reads as an instruction. A CLAUDE.md rule is itself just more text in the same context, so it can be overridden or ignored; you need mechanisms too: read-only roles, deny rules, code paths that never execute data, and a guard that reports rather than obeys.

questions.q: List three layers from OpenAI's guardrail stack and what each catches.
questions.a: Any three of: relevance classifier (off-topic inputs), safety classifier (jailbreaks and prompt injections), PII filter (exposing personal data), moderation (harmful content), rules-based protections (blocklists, regex, length limits), output validation (off-brand or invalid responses), tool safeguards (risk-rated tools that pause or escalate before high-risk actions).

questions.q: What makes your guild's run repeatable and auditable?
questions.a: Fixed input file, cached raw API responses reused on re-runs, one log line per row with status and reason, a run ID, and a stop after the first three rows for inspection.

questions.q: How does the sentinel-bird analogy break for prompt injection?
questions.a: Birds evaluate alarm calls as signals and learn to ignore unreliable callers. A model receives instructions and data as the same kind of tokens and doesn't learn across sessions which sources lie, so the separation has to be built into the harness.

modules.built: A logged, repeatable taxonomy-checking guild (planner, lookup, checker, guard, logger) that survived a planted injection and was checked by an independent reviewer: your Unit 5 build.

modules.title: Appendages: tool definitions, schemas and constrained decoding
objectives: Write a JSON-schema tool definition
Explain how constrained decoding guarantees well-formed calls
Design tools that are hard to misuse
modules.analogy: Appendage morphology fits function: beak shape predicts diet
modules.lab: Define three tools (taxonomy lookup, file read, unit converter) for your agent and watch how the model chooses between them.

questions.q: Give one tool a model fundamentally needs and one that merely helps, with reasons.
questions.a: Needs: anything fresher than its training data or private to you (today's date, a database query, your files), because its parameters are frozen. Helps: a calculator or code execution, because the model can reason through arithmetic but slowly and less reliably.

questions.q: What four properties must a valid tool call satisfy, and what can express all of them?
questions.a: Syntax (parses as JSON), shape (required fields present), types (each field has the right type) and allowed values (e.g. units in an enum). JSON Schema expresses all four.

questions.q: How does constrained decoding guarantee well-formed output, and what can still go wrong?
questions.a: The schema becomes a grammar; at each step the engine masks every token that would make the output invalid (score set to minus infinity) and renormalises over valid tokens. It can still fail if generation runs out of tokens mid-object, and it never guarantees the call is semantically right.

questions.q: Name three design choices that make a tool hard to misuse.
questions.a: Any three of: narrow scope (read only inside `data/`), enums and required fields, distinct non-overlapping names and descriptions, structured error messages that say what's wrong and what's allowed, risk ratings with pauses before high-risk calls, and deferring rarely used tools instead of loading all of them.

questions.q: Why is “tools are like beaks” misleading?
questions.a: Beaks are fixed and their fit was tested by selection; tools are added or removed per task with no testing unless you do it. Models choose tools by reading descriptions, so ambiguous wording causes wrong choices, and every tool description costs context on every turn.

modules.built: Three schema-defined tools with a validator that returns teaching errors, and a choice test that measures how well a model picks and fills them, the tool kit your capstone agents will carry.

modules.title: Learned behaviour: skills, SKILL.md and self-rewriting skill libraries
objectives: Write a SKILL.md with a name, description and on-demand body
Explain progressive disclosure for skills
Describe agents that induce or rewrite their own skills
modules.analogy: Learned behaviours and cultural transmission (song learning)
modules.lab: Write a “field-data-qc” skill and have Claude Code invoke it on a messy CSV; then ask it to improve the skill and compare versions.

questions.q: When should a procedure become a skill rather than a line in CLAUDE.md or a subagent?
questions.a: When you keep pasting the same instructions or multi-step procedure, or a CLAUDE.md section has grown into a procedure rather than a fact. Use a subagent instead when the work needs its own context or restricted permissions; a skill adds a procedure to the current worker without creating a new one.

questions.q: Explain progressive disclosure for skills in one or two sentences.
questions.a: Only each skill's name and description sit in context all the time; the full body loads when the skill is invoked, and supporting files load only if the body points to them. So a large library costs little until a skill is actually used.

questions.q: Why did Agent Workflow Memory use a judge before storing an induced workflow?
questions.a: Because storing workflows from incorrect trajectories would steer the agent wrong on future tasks. The judge predicts whether a trajectory succeeded so that only (probably) correct workflows enter memory.

questions.q: Your skill v2 beats v1 on the three files used to improve it but not on the held-out file. What happened?
questions.a: The edits were tuned to the training files (overfitting / teaching to the test). The held-out file is the honest measure; keep v1, or improve v2 using more varied examples and re-test on fresh held-out data.

questions.q: How does a self-rewriting skill library differ from song learning?
questions.a: Song learning checks output against a template and has population-level selection on which versions spread. A self-rewriting agent has neither unless you add them, so it can drift and store errors. You supply the selection with judges, tests, with/without comparisons and held-out sets.

modules.built: A `field-data-qc` skill with on-demand supporting files, an eval that compares with-skill, without-skill and two skill versions on held-out data, and the habit of treating a skill edit as an experiment.

modules.title: Shared interfaces: MCP servers, gateways and mods
objectives: Explain MCP as a shared interface standard between agents and tools
Describe the gateway/registry pattern at company scale
Customise an agent with plugins, hooks or mods
modules.analogy: Mutualism via a shared signal: pollinators and flowers converge on standard cues
modules.lab: Add one public MCP server to Claude Code, use it in a task, and write a small hook that blocks a dangerous command.

questions.q: In one sentence each, what are MCP and a skill, and how do they differ?
questions.a: MCP is a wire protocol through which an agent discovers and calls tools exposed by a separately running server. A skill is a folder of instructions and scripts the agent reads directly from disk. MCP connects to an external process; a skill packages expertise for the agent itself.

questions.q: What does “discovery doesn't imply exposure” mean in Uber's gateway, and why does it matter?
questions.a: Tools generated automatically from existing APIs start disabled; the owning team must review the descriptions and enable them. It stops unreviewed (possibly wrong or dangerous) tools from becoming available to agents just because a crawler found them.

questions.q: Why can't an agent simply load all 5,000 tools, and what pattern solves it?
questions.a: Every tool definition takes context on every turn, so thousands of them would swamp the window and cost a fortune. Progressive discovery solves it: a few meta-tools to find a server, list its tools, fetch one schema and invoke it, so only what's needed enters context.

questions.q: What are the three things a Claude Code mod hook can do with an event?
questions.a: Observe it (let it through and look at the result), rewrite it (change the event before Claude Code acts on it), or answer it (respond itself without passing it on, for example denying a tool call).

questions.q: Why is “MCP is like a pollination syndrome” only half true?
questions.a: Both are shared signals that let many partners interoperate. But mutualisms co-evolve slowly with cheaters policed by ecology, while an MCP server, possibly untrusted, can be added in seconds and its descriptions and responses flow straight into the agent's context. Trust must be managed explicitly with review, least privilege and guards.

modules.built: A project-scoped MCP browser connection used read-only on a public page, plus a tested PreToolUse guard that blocks destructive commands: with yesterday's skill, your Unit 6 build.

modules.title: Foraging for facts: BM25 keyword search and chunking
objectives: Explain BM25 scoring (term frequency, rarity, length normalisation)
Compare chunking strategies
Judge a ranked hit list for relevance (precision@5)
modules.analogy: Optimal foraging and the marginal value theorem: when to leave a patch
modules.lab: Use this pack’s corpus/query.py as your first RAG system: write 10 questions, label top-5 hits, then have your coding agent tune k1/b and compare.

questions.q: In BM25, what do idf, k1 and b each control?
questions.a: idf rewards rare, informative words over common ones; k1 sets how quickly extra repetitions of a word stop adding score (saturation); b sets how strongly long chunks are penalised for being long (0 = no penalty, 1 = full).

questions.q: Give two reasons the production RAG course builds keyword search before vector search.
questions.a: Keywords excel at exact technical terms, IDs and precise phrases; results are interpretable (you can see why something matched); and it's fast with no embedding model needed.

questions.q: What's the core trade-off in choosing chunk size, and what does overlap buy you?
questions.a: Large chunks lose retrieval precision (one chunk covers many topics), small chunks lose context (the idea is split). Overlap repeats text across chunk boundaries so an answer straddling a boundary isn't lost.

questions.q: Your question “How do agents forget earlier rules?” gets poor hits, but the pack covers compaction well. What's the likely failure and what are two fixes?
questions.a: A wording mismatch: BM25 only matches exact words, so “forget” doesn't hit “compaction”. Fixes: rewrite the query with the field's vocabulary, add embedding-based search (m21), or retrieve more and rerank.

questions.q: How does BM25 differ from a forager applying the marginal value theorem?
questions.a: A forager learns patch quality from experience; BM25 never learns and always gives the same ranking. It's blind to synonyms, and it doesn't account for diminishing returns from redundant chunks the agent has already read.

modules.built: A labelled 10-question eval set over this course's own corpus, a precision@5 baseline for BM25, and a tuning script that shows how much (or how little) k1 and b matter.

modules.title: Smelling the patch: embeddings and hybrid search
objectives: Explain embeddings and similarity search
Fuse keyword and vector rankings (reciprocal rank fusion)
A/B test retrieval changes on your own question set
modules.analogy: Olfactory search: following a gradient of similarity rather than an exact match
modules.lab: With your coding agent, add a small free embedding model to the pack search, fuse with BM25, and compare precision@5 with the m20 baseline.

questions.q: What is a text embedding, and how is similarity usually measured?
questions.a: A vector representation of text in a high-dimensional space where texts with similar meaning lie close together; similarity is usually cosine similarity, the angle between two vectors.

questions.q: Give one thing BM25 does better than embeddings and one thing embeddings do better.
questions.a: BM25: exact terms, names, IDs and numbers, with interpretable matches. Embeddings: paraphrases and synonyms, finding relevant passages that share no words with the query.

questions.q: Why does reciprocal rank fusion use ranks instead of raw scores?
questions.a: BM25 scores and cosine similarities are on different, incomparable scales. Ranks put both lists on the same footing, so documents high in both lists rise, and a document strong in only one list still gets credit.

questions.q: You switch to a better embedding model next month. What must you do, and why?
questions.a: Re-embed every chunk with the new model (and embed queries with the same model). Vectors from different models live in different spaces and can't be compared.

questions.q: Why is “embeddings are a sense of smell” misleading?
questions.a: Smell follows a real chemical gradient tied to the resource. Embedding similarity is learned from text statistics, so a fluent passage on the right topic that doesn't answer the question can rank highly. You only find out by checking hits against labelled questions.

modules.built: An embedding index over the course corpus (or a candidate pool), a hybrid BM25-plus-vector retriever with reciprocal rank fusion, and a labelled A/B test showing where each sense wins.

modules.title: The field notebook: agent memory and second brains
objectives: Distinguish working context, compaction and external memory
Organise a markdown knowledge base with an index file
Test recall with questions you already know the answers to
modules.analogy: Field notebooks and herbaria: external memory that outlives the expedition
modules.lab: Build a markdown field notebook of your paper notes with a CLAUDE.md index and /process, /ask commands; test recall on 10 known answers.

questions.q: Name the three layers of agent memory and one weakness of each.
questions.a: Working context (limited, wiped between sessions, early instructions get lost as it fills); compaction (lossy summaries that get lossier with repetition and can drop mid-conversation instructions); external memory (only as good as what's written and how it's found, and it can store and reinforce errors).

questions.q: What did CMU's compaction story teach about evaluating memory?
questions.a: A compaction method that cost nothing on a benchmark still caused real failures (repeating the same pull request, forgetting mid-conversation instructions) because the benchmark didn't represent those situations. Memory needs realistic tests, not just benchmark scores.

questions.q: What does MemGPT borrow from computer operating systems, and what did Mem0 add?
questions.a: A memory hierarchy: a small, fast working context inside the window and a large, slow external store, with reads and writes made by the model's own tool calls. Mem0 added updating and deleting stored facts when new information contradicts or replaces them.

questions.q: Why “one topic per file, named for its content” in a second brain?
questions.a: The agent finds things through the map and filenames, so a descriptive name and a single topic make the right file easy to locate and cite; mixed files and names like `note-12.md` hide information and invite wrong retrievals.

questions.q: Why can't you treat agent memory like a herbarium?
questions.a: A herbarium specimen is fixed and checkable; agent memory is rewritten by the agent, so misreadings can be stored, cited and reinforced, and summaries of summaries have no original to return to. Keep raw inputs archived, forbid deletion, and audit with known-answer questions.

modules.built: A Markdown field notebook with a `CLAUDE.md` map, `/process` and `/ask` commands, and a 10-question recall test with code-checked citations: your Unit 7 build and the capstone's memory.

modules.title: Designing a fitness assay: evals and hill-climbing
objectives: Design tasks that mirror real use with headroom
Keep a held-out split and check grader agreement
Hill-climb a prompt or config against the eval without overfitting
modules.analogy: Common-garden experiments: measure fitness under controlled conditions
modules.lab: Write a 30-item eval for a small task in your field with a code grader; hill-climb a prompt with your coding agent and report train vs held-out scores.

questions.q: Name the four properties of a well-designed eval from Anthropic's guide.
questions.a: Tasks mirror the real (production) distribution; stronger models and more thinking score higher; there is passable headroom (the best setup is well below 100%, but not because of impossible tasks); and run-to-run variance is low.

questions.q: Why is it a bad idea to build an eval from the cases today's model gets wrong?
questions.a: Capability is jagged, so you'd be sampling the valleys of one model's capability surface. The eval would measure that model's failure fingerprint rather than what is genuinely hard or valuable for your work. Pick hard cases because a human judged them hard, and be able to say why.

questions.q: During hill-climbing your train score rises from 70% to 85% but the held-out score stays at 70%. What do you do, and why?
questions.a: Revert the change. Train improving while test stays flat is the classic sign of overfitting: the change fitted quirks of the training items rather than improving the task in general.

questions.q: The score stalls for three rounds. What does the guide recommend instead of another edit?
questions.a: Stop editing and sort every remaining train failure by cause. This often reveals ambiguous tasks, broken graders or harness errors, which you fix in the eval itself, rather than spending rounds on changes too small to measure.

questions.q: You improved test accuracy from 7/10 to 8/10. Should you merge the change?
questions.a: Not on that evidence. One item out of ten is well within the noise of a 10-item set (the confidence intervals overlap heavily). Add items or repeated runs until the eval's noise is smaller than the improvement you care about.

modules.built: A 30-item, expert-checked eval with a code grader, a train/test split, confidence intervals and a logged hill-climb: the first component of your capstone's eval suite.

modules.title: Judges, RAG metrics and tracing
objectives: Choose between code graders and LLM-as-judge
Use faithfulness and context precision/recall for RAG
Debug with traces instead of guesses
modules.analogy: Inter-observer reliability when scoring behaviour
modules.lab: Score your m21 retrieval pipeline with an open-source eval library using a free or local judge, and inspect five traces.

questions.q: When should you use an LLM judge rather than a code grader?
questions.a: Only when outputs are open-ended (many valid answers) but there are clear quality criteria. If outputs are constrained (a label, a schema, tests), a code grader is cheaper, deterministic and can't share the system's biases.

questions.q: List three practices that make an LLM judge more trustworthy.
questions.a: Any three of: a rubric written as checkable claims rather than a 1-5 scale; binary verdicts; a judge model different from the one being tested; blind, randomly ordered pairwise comparisons; running the judge twice on the same output to check stability; comparing its verdicts with your own labels (agreement or kappa) before trusting it.

questions.q: Your RAG answers score high on faithfulness but low on contextual recall. What's wrong, and where do you fix it?
questions.a: The generator is faithfully summarising the evidence it got, but the retriever isn't fetching what the answer needs. Fix retrieval (more candidates, hybrid search, better chunking, query rewriting), not the generation prompt.

questions.q: Why isn't "no errors in the logs" a good sign that an agent run went well?
questions.a: Because the failure that matters is usually a quality failure, not a crash: the call returns successfully with a wrong or hallucinated answer. You need traces that record inputs, retrieved context and outputs so you can check the content, plus evals that score it.

questions.q: Give one way the inter-observer analogy breaks for LLM judges.
questions.a: Human observers can be trained against each other and their errors are fairly independent. An LLM judge shares training data and blind spots with the generator and can prefer text like its own, so judge-generator agreement can mean both are wrong in the same way. Calibrate against your own labels.

modules.built: A traced RAG evaluation with four metrics, a judge from a different model family, and a measured judge-versus-you agreement score: the scoring layer of your capstone's eval suite.

modules.title: The Red Queen: independent verification and adversarial testing
objectives: Never let the generator grade its own homework
Add verifier and adversary agents
Report results with confidence intervals
modules.analogy: Coevolutionary arms races (Red Queen): predators and prey keep each other honest
modules.lab: Add an independent verifier that checks claims against citations; measure how many planted errors it catches versus self-checking.

questions.q: Why does a verifier need a fresh context rather than the worker's conversation?
questions.a: A verifier that has seen the worker's reasoning is primed to accept it and tends to agree with everything. Given only the claim and the evidence in a new session, it judges the claim on its merits.

questions.q: Your three verifiers all agree a figure is correct, but all three checked it against the same summary the worker produced. What's wrong?
questions.a: They share an upstream source, so their agreement is an echo, not independent confirmation. You need an anchor outside the model chain: the original data, the primary source, or a test that actually runs.

questions.q: How do you check that a judge or verifier isn't blind?
questions.a: Break something on purpose. Plant known errors (or feed a known-bad output) and confirm the checker flags them, while keeping known-good items. Report catch rate and false-alarm rate.

questions.q: A verifier catches 5 of 6 planted errors and self-checking catches 3 of 6. Can you conclude the verifier is better?
questions.a: Not confidently. With n = 6 the 95% intervals are very wide and overlap heavily. Plant more errors or repeat across several reports before claiming a difference.

questions.q: How does the Red Queen analogy break for adversarial evals?
questions.a: Natural arms races have independent opponents and no referee. In evals you build both sides, so a weak adversary (same model, same context, same sources as the generator) can give false comfort. You have to measure the adversary's strength, for example with planted errors.

modules.built: `checkers.py`: an independent claim verifier and a three-lens adversary, with a planted-error benchmark showing how much more they catch than self-checking. This completes the Unit 8 build: an eval suite with a held-out split (m23), a calibrated judge (m24) and an adversarial checker (m25), all reused in the capstone.

modules.title: Domestication at home: running models locally
objectives: Explain quantisation and memory needs (weights + context cache)
Run a small open model locally and measure tokens per second
Know when local models are good enough
modules.analogy: Domestic strains: smaller, hardier, adapted to your environment
modules.lab: With your coding agent, install a local runtime, run a 1-4B model, change one setting at a time and log speed and memory.

questions.q: What decides which models you can load, and what decides how fast they generate?
questions.a: Memory size decides what loads (weights plus context cache plus headroom must fit). Memory bandwidth sets the ceiling on tokens per second, because every active weight is read from memory once per generated token.

questions.q: Your 4-bit model fits easily, but when you raise the context window to the full length it runs out of memory. Why?
questions.a: The context (KV) cache grows with the context window, and it's a separate memory cost on top of the weights. At long contexts it can be many gigabytes. Use a smaller window, quantise the KV cache, or use a smaller model file.

questions.q: A compressed model is advertised at "98% of the original". Why should you still test it on your own eval?
questions.a: An average over many benchmarks can hide a big drop on a particular kind of task. In the pack's example the same compressed model scored far lower on a long-horizon agent benchmark. Agentic, multi-step tasks tend to degrade before trivia does.

questions.q: What's the difference between prefill and decode speed, and which one makes long documents feel slow?
questions.a: Prefill is how fast the model reads your prompt; decode is how fast it writes the answer. Long inputs are dominated by prefill, which many apps don't show you.

questions.q: Why is "quantisation is like domestication" misleading?
questions.a: Domestication adapts a strain to your conditions through selection. Quantisation is lossy compression of the same generalist model: nothing is adapted to your tasks. Adapting it requires fine-tuning on your own examples.

modules.built: A local model running on your own machine, a `bench.csv` of speed and memory under controlled one-setting changes, and a first measurement of whether it's good enough for your m23 task.

modules.title: Selective breeding: supervised fine-tuning and LoRA
objectives: Explain SFT as imitation of demonstrations
Explain LoRA as cheap, small adaptations on a frozen base
Fine-tune a small classifier and compare it with the base model
modules.analogy: Artificial selection from a breeding stock; cultural transmission by imitation
modules.lab: Run a free notebook to fine-tune a small model as a classifier for your field (e.g. study type from abstract), and compare base vs tuned accuracy on held-out data.

questions.q: In SFT, which tokens does the loss count, and why?
questions.a: Only the assistant's (model-generated) tokens. Prompts and tool outputs are context, not things the model should learn to produce; minimising loss on the response tokens raises the probability of each demonstrated action given its context.

questions.q: Give two limits of SFT from the CMU lecture.
questions.a: Any two of: it can't exceed its teacher; it inherits demonstrations that are wrong or narrow; it copies bad habits that appear in successful examples; gains level off with more examples of the same tasks; training loss can look fine while real performance doesn't improve.

questions.q: What does LoRA change and what does it leave alone?
questions.a: It freezes the base model's weights and trains small low-rank adapter matrices added to chosen layers (plus, in decision models, a small scoring head). The adapter is small, cheap to train and can be stored and swapped separately.

questions.q: Why train on synthetic examples but test only on your human-checked items?
questions.a: The test must reflect the real distribution and must be correct. Synthetic items can be easier, biased towards the generator's style, or mislabelled; testing on them would overstate performance. Decontaminate so no test item (or near copy) leaks into training.

questions.q: Kev reports that fine-tuning from the base model scored far lower on its general evaluation than fine-tuning from the released checkpoint. What lesson applies to your own fine-tunes?
questions.a: Start from a model that already has the capability you want and add your domain on top; and always evaluate abilities you weren't trying to change, because a narrow fine-tune can erase them.

modules.built: A filtered synthetic training set, a Colab notebook that fine-tunes a small decision model with LoRA, and a base-versus-tuned comparison on your human-checked held-out items: the selective-breeding step of your capstone's cheap "reflex" layer.

modules.title: Selection on behaviour: reinforcement learning basics
objectives: Explain rollouts, rewards and policy updates
Connect evals to rewards (and reward hacking to Goodhart’s law)
Understand why RL for agents is hard
modules.analogy: Natural selection acting on behaviour; Goodhart’s law as selection on a proxy trait
modules.lab: Run a tiny RL demo (a free notebook or a toy script your coding agent writes) with a verifiable reward; plot reward over time and look for hacking.

questions.q: Define policy, rollout and reward in one sentence each.
questions.a: The policy is the model's probability distribution over the next action given the history. A rollout is one complete episode of actions and observations. The reward is a single number scoring how good that episode was.

questions.q: What does subtracting a baseline do, and how does GRPO get its baseline?
questions.a: It turns raw reward into an advantage (better or worse than expected), which reduces the variance of the update without biasing it. GRPO runs a group of rollouts on the same task and uses the group's mean reward as the baseline, so no separate value model is needed.

questions.q: Why does RL fail to learn on tasks where every rollout fails?
questions.a: With every reward equal, the advantages are all zero, so there's no signal about which actions were better. RL can only amplify behaviour the policy already sometimes produces; you need easier tasks, hints, demonstrations or an SFT cold start first.

questions.q: In the lab's buggy condition, reward rose to near 1 while true success fell. Name this and connect it to Goodhart's law.
questions.a: Reward hacking: the policy optimised the measure (the buggy verifier) instead of the goal (finding the number). Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Selection on a proxy trait gives you the proxy.

questions.q: Why does your Unit 8 eval work matter for RL?
questions.a: A verifier that grades outputs is exactly what an RL loop optimises, so every grader flaw becomes a target. Robust, independent, adversarially tested graders (m23-m25) are what make a reward safe to optimise, and they must keep co-evolving as the policy improves.

modules.built: A from-scratch policy-gradient learner with a baseline, a live demonstration of reward hacking, and `decide.py`: a gated local decision layer your capstone router can call. This completes the Unit 9 build.

modules.title: Agents with bodies: simulation, self-practice and robot data
objectives: Describe agents writing and testing robot code with simulation in the loop
Explain the robot data pyramid (simulation, teleoperation, video)
Report robot success rates with confidence intervals
modules.analogy: Reciprocal transplant experiments: does performance transfer to a new environment?
modules.lab: Ask your coding agent to write a small MuJoCo reach or gait task on CPU, tune it, and report success rate with a confidence interval. Link to your robotics course for depth.

questions.q: What are the two problems SimEX identifies with putting coding agents directly on robots?
questions.a: Writing control code in one pass fails because the model must guess physical quantities it can't know (calibration, reachable grasps). Iterating on the physical robot is slow, costly and potentially unsafe, since every trial uses robot time and untested code can collide.

questions.q: Why can SimEX work with a simulator that is only "roughly correct"?
questions.a: Because it transfers knowledge and procedures (a toolbox of primitives plus measured limits and strategies), not one policy fitted to one simulated scene; and it corrects the simulator with a few real trials in Stage 2.

questions.q: In the Robotics Data Map, what's on the other side of "the fence", and why does it matter?
questions.a: Rollouts: data where the policy, not a human, is acting. Only rollouts contain the policy's own mistakes, which is the signal that teaches recovery; human demonstrations, however close to the robot's action space, can't supply it.

questions.q: A paper reports 9/10 real-robot successes. What should you ask?
questions.a: For the interval and the protocol: how many trials, seeds and tasks, whether evaluation tasks were held out, and the confidence interval. 9/10 has a wide 95% interval (roughly 60% to 98%).

questions.q: How does the reciprocal-transplant analogy break for sim-to-real?
questions.a: Transplanted organisms keep adapting and the home site is real. A sim-trained controller has a fixed gap to a reality it never saw, and can exploit simulator inaccuracies, so the gap only closes through better simulation, real data or an explicit adaptation step.

modules.built: A simulated reaching controller your coding agent wrote, tuned, scored with intervals on held-out targets, and transplanted to perturbed physics: the Unit 10 build.

modules.title: Choosing your niche: AI for science and the impedance mismatch
objectives: Identify problems where AI output can be verified
Audit a real workflow before automating it
Scope a capstone that reuses each unit’s build
modules.analogy: Niche construction: organisms that reshape their environment to fit
modules.lab: Audit one of your lab workflows step by step (delete / rule / agent / human) with your coding agent and write the capstone spec.

questions.q: What does Schwartz mean by an "impedance mismatch" between scientists and AI?
questions.a: Both systems work well on their own but are poorly matched: treating the model like a human collaborator doesn't draw out its strengths (breadth, coding, maths and statistics, reading data fast), so much of the effort never gets through. The fix is to find problems shaped to what it does well.

questions.q: In the neutral-theory project, what did the ecologist add that the model didn't?
questions.a: Taste and direction. The model's result was technically impressive but would have been "met with a shrug", because ecologists already knew neutral theory falls short; the expert's idea to study the residual from the neutral prediction turned it into interesting science.

questions.q: Name the four buckets for sorting workflow steps, with one example each from your field.
questions.a: Delete (a step that's pure theatre, such as re-typing data already in a spreadsheet); plain code (a range check on a measurement); agent (judging whether an abstract is relevant to your project, given past decisions); human (approving the final dataset or a submission).

questions.q: Why can speeding up every step of a process achieve almost nothing?
questions.a: Because most elapsed time is often in queues, handoffs and exception loops, not the work itself (Hammer's 22 days containing 17 minutes of work). Removing steps and loops matters more than accelerating them.

questions.q: What makes a capstone problem "verifiable", and why does it matter?
questions.a: Its outputs can be checked against something independent of the model: a schema, a test, a source passage, labelled examples or a known value. Without that anchor, your evals, verifiers and rewards have nothing solid to measure against.

modules.built: A real process map with every step sorted into delete / code / agent / human, a baseline plan, and a one-page capstone spec that assigns each earlier unit build a job.

modules.title: Assembling the ecosystem: harness, specialists and memory
objectives: Assemble harness, router, specialist agents and RAG memory into one system
Wire components through clear interfaces
Keep a map (CLAUDE.md) of the whole system
modules.analogy: Community assembly: species arrive, interact and form a stable community
modules.lab: With your coding agent, combine your unit builds into a literature-triage and field-data-QA team for one real dataset.

questions.q: What are the seven parts every harness shares, according to the Wavestone study?
questions.a: Loop, LLM layer, tools, memory, safety, orchestration and extensions (hooks, skills, MCP). Harnesses differ in the size of each part, not in having them.

questions.q: "The loop lives inside a node; the graph lives between them." What goes in each?
questions.a: Inside a node: produce, check, correct, repeat until the check passes (with a cap). Between nodes: splitting, fanning out, merging (in code), gating and sending failed units back.

questions.q: One of four parallel slices fails its check. What should go back, and with what?
questions.a: Only the failing slice, with its verdict, the reason, the evidence and a scope line limiting the fix to that slice. Sending the whole batch back rewrites correct work, adds new uncertainty and can stop the run converging.

questions.q: What makes a handoff between agents robust?
questions.a: It's a file at a known path with a fixed shape (schema), a named sender and receiver, a definition of done for the next stage, and a stated behaviour for incomplete payloads, rather than intent reconstructed from a chat.

questions.q: Why is "community assembly" an imperfect analogy for building this system?
questions.a: Natural communities assemble themselves and unspecified interactions can still stabilise. Your system only has the interactions you build; untested edges fail silently (for example two agents overwriting one file), so every edge needs a contract and every node a check.

modules.built: A working capstone pipeline: router, two specialists with internal loops, a code-node merge, an independent verification gate, one human approval point, explicit file handoffs, and a map plus four state files, dry-run on real data.

modules.title: Stress-testing the ecosystem: evals, adversaries and budgets
objectives: Run the eval suite and adversarial agent against the full system
Set and monitor a cost and latency budget
Decide what to ship and what to cut
modules.analogy: Disturbance experiments: perturb the community and measure resilience
modules.lab: Run the full eval + adversary suite, compute cost per task, write a one-page report, and plan the next iteration.

questions.q: Why judge an agent on the worst of three runs rather than a single run?
questions.a: Agents are non-deterministic, so one green run says little. Per-attempt success multiplies down quickly (75% per attempt gives about 42% for three in a row), and an unattended system needs to succeed every time, not once.

questions.q: Name four disturbances worth testing in a literature-triage and field-QA system.
questions.a: Any four of: malformed or empty input files, missing columns, swapped units, an injected instruction inside an abstract, an unavailable retrieval index, a timed-out model call, planted errors in the output report.

questions.q: Why report median, mean and p90 cost rather than just the average?
questions.a: Costs are skewed. The median shows the typical task, the mean is pulled by expensive outliers, and the p90 shows the tail that blows budgets. LangChain's router reported all three so the savings couldn't come from a few cheap outliers alone.

questions.q: Your new component improves held-out accuracy from 80% to 83%, with overlapping intervals, at twice the cost. Ship it?
questions.a: No. The gain is within noise, so it isn't demonstrated, and it doubles cost. Either gather more evidence (more items, more runs) or cut it. Anthropic's guide recommends against merging gains within noise.

questions.q: How does the disturbance-experiment analogy break for agent systems?
questions.a: Ecosystems recover on their own through intrinsic processes. An agent system has no recovery except what you build, and it usually degrades silently while still producing fluent output, so evals and monitoring must run continuously.

modules.built: A one-command eval and disturbance suite for your whole capstone, a cost-and-latency profile against a budget you set in advance, and a one-page report with ship/cut decisions and the next iteration planned. Your ecosystem is built, assayed and stress-tested.
